title: Short Stuff: William A. Mitchell: Food Inventor
summary: Short Stuff episode on food scientist William A. Mitchell (1911–2004), a research chemist for about thirty-five years at General Foods who held more than seventy food patents. The hosts cover his Minnesota farm childhood, his early work with sugar and corn, a lab explosion that left him with severe burns, and his best-known products: Tang powdered drink, quick-set cold-water Jell-O, Cool Whip, an attempt at instant carbonated Kool-Aid that led to Pop Rocks, and a 1970s open letter defending Pop Rocks safety. They also note his daughter Cheryl Mitchell, also a food scientist, and close with a sign-off.

entities.name: Agricultural Experiment Station in Lincoln, Nebraska

segments.title: Introduction to William A. Mitchell
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Mitchell as a General Foods research chemist who stayed in the lab rather than accept management promotions.

segments.title: Mitchell's farm childhood and early work
segments.summary: Mitchell was born in 1911 to a Minnesota farm family. After his father died, he worked in farm labor, trapped muskrats, and harvested melons as a teen, and he worked his way through college.

segments.title: Sugar tank job and early research career
segments.summary: Mitchell worked the overnight shift at the sugar crystallization tank room for the American Beet Sugar Company. After earning a master's degree in chemistry, he began research at the Agricultural Experiment Station in Lincoln, Nebraska, on food and corn.

segments.title: Lab explosion and move to General Foods
segments.summary: A cracked beaker heated with alcohol exploded, causing second and third degree burns over most of Mitchell's body. After a few months of recovery, he took a job and moved to White Plains, New York, with General Foods.

segments.title: Transition to famous inventions
segments.summary: The hosts set up a break and note that the discussion will turn to his best-known foods, which they say are not health foods.

segments.title: Tang and its space program fame
segments.summary: Mitchell developed Tang, a powdered citrus-flavored drink that is mostly sugar with some vitamin C and turns bright orange when mixed with water. It was carried on John Glenn's Mercury flight in 1962 and was a sponsor of the Apollo 8 broadcast.

segments.title: Buzz Aldrin's criticism of Tang
segments.summary: Buzz Aldrin later said Tang sucks, remarks made while presenting an award to Felix Baumgartner at a 2013 Spike TV Guy's Choice event. Glenn had earlier said the flavor of the space water was poor.

segments.title: Hosts' childhood memories of Tang and Kool-Aid
segments.summary: The hosts talk about childhood drinks, including Tang, Kool-Aid, and the large amounts of sugar used when making Kool-Aid at home.

segments.title: Cold-water quick-set Jell-O and Cool Whip
segments.summary: Mitchell patented a quick-set Jell-O that uses cold water in 1967 to save time. He also contributed to Cool Whip, a mostly artificial whipped topping that became freezable because it has no milk product in its original formulation. The hosts discuss the ingredient list and how they use it.

segments.title: Whipped cream comparison and peanut butter joke
segments.summary: The hosts compare Cool Whip with aerosol whipped cream and joke about combining Cool Whip with peanut butter.

segments.title: Instant carbonated Kool-Aid and the origin of Pop Rocks
segments.summary: In 1956 Mitchell tried to carbonate Kool-Aid to make instant soda. He shelved the project, and about twenty years later someone else modified the process to create Pop Rocks.

segments.title: Pop Rocks description and personal anecdote
segments.summary: Pop Rocks are small candies that crackle as carbon dioxide releases in the mouth. Chuck describes giving them to his daughter Ruby.

segments.title: Pop Rocks and soda stomach myth
segments.summary: A myth held that eating Pop Rocks with soda could make your stomach explode. General Foods ran a 1970s full-page open letter, written by Mitchell, to reassure parents that the combination is safe.

segments.title: Mitchell's later life and daughter Cheryl Mitchell
segments.summary: Mitchell retired from General Foods in 1976, had seven children, and was married for sixty years. He died in 2004. His daughter Cheryl Mitchell is also a food scientist, known for rice milk and Elmhurst products.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with a salute to Mitchell and end Short Stuff.

segments.title: Show credits
segments.summary: Closing credits note that Stuff You Should Know is an iHeartRadio production and point to other podcasts.
